sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses abuse, forced treatment, restraint and deaths in psychiatric hospitals. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: What this page covers
sections.heading: What this page covers
sections.body:
This page covers psychiatric hospitals and psych wards for adults and young people, whether or not a hospital is also part of the troubled teen industry. Many youth programs we track sit on a psychiatric hospital's campus, carry its name and its owner, or are a unit inside it. Those programs are in [our directory](/tti-program-index/).

The hospitals and the teen programs are one business. The same companies own both and run both the same way: people who cannot leave are kept to fill beds, with too few staff, and are restrained, secluded and drugged.

We are not the experts on psychiatric hospitals. The organizations listed below are, and many of them are run by people who have been hospitalized themselves.

sections.label: Locked in
sections.heading: Locked in
sections.body:
A psychiatric admission is often not a choice. Every state lets a person be held for an emergency evaluation and lets a court order a longer commitment. The rules and time limits differ from state to state, and no one counts the holds nationally. In 24 states with about half the country's population, there were about 591,000 emergency detentions in 2014, 357 for every 100,000 people. In the 22 of them with data from 2012 to 2016, detentions rose 13 percent while the population grew 4 percent.[^1]

A patient who is held cannot leave until the hospital or a court lets them go. A hospital paid for every day a bed is filled has a reason to keep them.

sections.label: Who holds them
sections.heading: Who holds them
sections.body:
When Medicare and Medicaid began in 1965, most inpatient psychiatric care was given in state and county hospitals. In the decades since, it has moved into private hands. By 2023 privately owned psychiatric hospitals accounted for 35 percent of the psychiatric hospital days Medicare paid for, and government-run ones for 4 percent; the rest were in the psych wards of general hospitals.[^2] For-profit hospitals are still gaining: from 2019 to 2024 they grew from about a fifth of Medicare's certified psychiatric facilities to over a quarter, while the total fell.[^3]

Table: Inpatient psychiatric care in the United States
| Measure | Figure |
|---|---|
| Psychiatric facilities certified by Medicare, 2024 | 1,430, down from 1,610 in 2019[^3] |
| Share that are psych wards of general hospitals, 2024 | 59 percent[^3] |
| Share that are free-standing for-profit hospitals, 2024 | Over a quarter, up from about a fifth in 2019[^3] |
| Medicare psychiatric hospital days in privately owned hospitals, 2023 | 35 percent[^2] |
| Medicare psychiatric hospital days in government-run hospitals, 2023 | 4 percent[^2] |
| Inpatient mental health beds, all ages, 2024 | 60,201[^4] |

The two largest for-profit chains are Universal Health Services (UHS) and Acadia Healthcare.

Table: The two largest for-profit chains
| | UHS | Acadia |
|---|---|---|
| Behavioral health facilities, end of 2025 | 182 in the U.S., 161 in the U.K., 3 in Puerto Rico[^5] | 277 in 40 states and Puerto Rico, over 12,500 beds[^6] |
| Youth programs in our records | [75](/operator/universal-health-services/) | [14](/operator/acadia-healthcare/) |
| Federal settlements | $122 million in 2020[^7] | $19.9 million in 2024[^6] |

sections.label: The same companies own the teen programs
sections.heading: The same companies own the teen programs
sections.body:
UHS's list of its own facilities puts psychiatric hospitals beside Provo Canyon School and Copper Hills Youth Center in Utah and Oak Plains Academy in Tennessee. Some share a name and a city: Cedar Ridge Behavioral Hospital and Cedar Ridge Residential Treatment Center in Oklahoma City, and North Star Hospital in Anchorage with the North Star DeBarr and Palmer residential treatment centers.[^5] About 60 programs in our records, under many owners, are named for a hospital or one of its units, such as Cedar Crest Hospital & RTC in Texas, Hampstead Hospital & RTC in New Hampshire and West Oaks Hospital PRTF in Texas.[^8] Medicaid pays for both under one rule, the inpatient psychiatric benefit for people under 21.[^9]

The chains bought their way into teen programs. Charter Behavioral Health Systems bought the original campus of Provo Canyon School in 1986, and by 1999 ran 91 hospitals treating 35,000 children and adolescents a year.[^10] When Charter went bankrupt in 2000, UHS bought 11 of its facilities, Provo Canyon School among them.[^11][^12] UHS added the Keystone youth programs and five former Brown Schools programs in 2005, and Acadia bought CRC Health Group, owner of Aspen Education Group's teen programs, in 2015.[^10] People moved the other way. In 1993 Robert Lichfield, who started as a dorm parent at Provo Canyon School and went on to found WWASP, took over the management of Brightway Adolescent Hospital in St. George, Utah; health officials said it promptly began sending young people to tough-love behavior programs.[^13]

The tie is older than the chains, because the teen program grew out of the hospital. The residential treatment center began as a psychiatric clinic's children's division, the Menninger Clinic's Southard School (1926).[^14] The group methods used on teenagers began as a way of running a psychiatric ward, the "therapeutic community" Tom Main named in 1946.[^15] They reached teenagers through Synanon, which grew out of its founder's part in an LSD study funded by the National Institute of Mental Health, and through programs psychiatrists started: Daniel Casriel co-founded Daytop Village (1964) with an NIMH grant, and Gerald Davidson co-founded Elan School (1971). The Seed, CEDU and Straight, Inc. carried the same methods into programs for teenagers.[^16]

Psychiatric units and other providers outside the troubled teen industry that use its practices or refer young people to it are on our [list of mental health providers](/mental-health-providers/).

sections.label: Kept to fill beds
sections.heading: Kept to fill beds
sections.body:
The Senate Finance Committee's 2024 investigation of youth residential treatment run by UHS, Acadia, Devereux and Vivant found that these providers "optimize per diems by filling large facilities to capacity and maximize profit by concurrently reducing the number and quality of staff" ([our summary](/warehouses-of-neglect/)).[^17] Staff and federal investigators describe the same business in the companies' psychiatric hospitals, and the public pays for it: Acadia received 57.7 percent of its 2025 revenue from Medicaid and 14.3 percent from Medicare.[^6]

At UHS, 175 current and former staff interviewed by BuzzFeed News in 2016 described pressure to fill beds and to keep patients until their insurance ran out. UHS rejected the allegations.[^18] In 2020 UHS paid $122 million to settle federal allegations that from 2006 to 2018 its behavioral health facilities admitted patients who did not need inpatient care, kept them longer than needed, understaffed, and improperly used physical and chemical restraints and seclusion. Liability was not determined. UHS signed a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement with an independent monitor for its behavioral health division.[^7]

At Acadia, more than 50 current and former executives and staff told The New York Times in 2024 that the company held patients against their will when it was not medically necessary, often for financial reasons. In at least 12 of the 19 states where Acadia runs psychiatric hospitals, patients, employees and police officers had alerted authorities.[^19] That September Acadia paid $19.9 million, admitting no liability, to settle a federal investigation of medical necessity, admissions, discharges, length of stay and patient care at several of its facilities.[^6] Since then it has received grand jury subpoenas from the Justice Department's Criminal Division about the admissions, length of stay and billing of its acute psychiatric hospitals, and subpoenas from the SEC. As of July 2026 the investigations were open and no findings had been made.[^20]

sections.label: Held down and drugged
sections.heading: Held down and drugged
sections.body:
Restraint has killed patients in these hospitals for decades. In 1998 the Hartford Courant's series "Deadly Restraint" counted 142 deaths tied to restraint or seclusion over ten years in psychiatric hospitals and wards, group homes and youth residential facilities.[^21] The next year *60 Minutes II* opened its report on Charter with Tristan Sovern, 16, asphyxiated while staff restrained him at a Charter hospital in Greensboro, North Carolina, the third patient in four months to die in restraints at a Charter hospital.[^22] Charter tried to block the broadcast in court and lost.[^10] Until 1999 no federal rule governed restraint and seclusion in psychiatric hospitals, and only 15 states had any system to alert their Protection and Advocacy agency to such deaths.[^21]

The federal rules now forbid restraint or seclusion "imposed as a means of coercion, discipline, convenience, or retaliation by staff," count a drug given to manage behavior outside standard treatment as a restraint, and require hospitals to report to CMS every death in restraint or seclusion or within 24 hours after it.[^23] Hospitals did not report them. Between August 1999 and December 2004 they failed to report 44 of 104 documented deaths, and CMS and state agencies often did not act in time on the deaths that were reported.[^24]

The practices go on. The UHS settlement covered improper restraint and seclusion.[^7] In 2024, asked whether a child could be chemically restrained and secluded at once, UHS personnel told Senate Finance Committee staff "there are no rules preventing doubling or tripling up on a restraint and seclusion," a practice federal regulations prohibit.[^17]

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If someone is in danger now**, call 911. For a mental health crisis, call or text [988](tel:988), the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, 24 hours a day.
- **Protection and Advocacy agency.** Every state and territory has one. Under the federal PAIMI program they investigate abuse, neglect and rights violations against people with mental illness in public and private facilities, including restraint and seclusion.[^25] Find yours in [NDRN's directory](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/).
- **State health department.** Hospitals are licensed by the state, and the state survey agency investigates complaints for Medicare and Medicaid. CMS lists [each state's complaint contact](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/health-safety-standards/quality-safety-oversight-general-information/contact-information).
- **The Joint Commission**, if the hospital is accredited by it: [report a safety concern online](https://www.jointcommission.org/en-us/contact-us/report-a-patient-safety-event) or call 1-800-994-6610. You can report anonymously.
- **A death in restraint or seclusion** must be reported by the hospital to CMS. You can also tell the state survey agency and the Protection and Advocacy agency yourself.
- For troubled teen programs, including youth residential treatment run by the same companies, use [our reporting directory](/report-abuse/).

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [MindFreedom International](https://mindfreedom.org/): A human rights organization in mental health care, with psychiatric survivors among its board and past leaders. It works against forced psychiatric treatment.
- [National Association for Rights Protection and Advocacy (NARPA)](https://www.narpa.org/): Supports people with psychiatric diagnoses in exercising their legal and human rights, and works to end forced treatment.
- [National Empowerment Center](https://power2u.org/): Works with people with lived experience of mental health issues, trauma and extreme states. It keeps directories of peer respites and peer-run warmlines.
- [Wildflower Alliance](https://wildfloweralliance.org/): A grassroots group in Western Massachusetts and online offering peer support, advocacy and training, including peer-run respites.
- [National Disability Rights Network (NDRN)](https://www.ndrn.org/): The national organization of the Protection and Advocacy agencies, the largest providers of legal advocacy for people with disabilities.
- [Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law](https://www.bazelon.org/): A national legal advocacy organization for the civil rights of people with mental disabilities, through lawsuits and policy work.
- [Mad in America](https://www.madinamerica.com/): A publication of the Mad in America Foundation with research news, original journalism and writing by people with lived experience of psychiatric care.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you have been hospitalized, work in psychiatric care or advocate in this field, and something on this page is wrong or missing, please [tell us](/contact/). We will change it.
